details:
**The green light**
The green light at the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock in East Egg, visible across the bay from Jay Gatsby's mansion in West Egg. Gatsby first appears stretching out his arms toward it "in a curious way," trembling. Once he is reunited with Daisy, Nick notes that its "colossal significance" has vanished and Gatsby's "count of enchanted objects had diminished by one." At the end Nick links it to "the orgastic future that year by year recedes before us," and it is usually read as a symbol of Gatsby's unreachable dream.

**The Valley of Ashes and the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg**
A bleak industrial wasteland between West Egg and New York City, watched over by a faded optometrist's billboard showing the huge spectacled eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg. George Wilson's garage is here, and after his wife's death George treats the eyes as the eyes of God. Francis Cugat's famous cover art of floating eyes and a face is often connected to the billboard.

**Myrtle Wilson's death**
Tom Buchanan's mistress Myrtle, the wife of the garage owner George Wilson, runs into the road and is killed by Gatsby's yellow car while Daisy is driving, so that her blood mixes with the ashes. Gatsby takes the blame to protect Daisy. The Greek neighbor Michaelis is the key witness to the accident.

**George Wilson shoots Gatsby in his pool**
After finding an expensive new dog leash that convinces him Myrtle was having an affair, George Wilson is told by Tom that the yellow car belonged to Gatsby. He shoots Gatsby as Gatsby floats in his swimming pool and then kills himself. A gardener finds the body, described as a "laden mattress," and the chapter ends "the holocaust was complete."

**Meyer Wolfsheim**
Gatsby's gangster associate and partner in bootlegging, who wears cufflinks made of human molars and is said to have fixed the 1919 World Series (the Black Sox Scandal). He offers Nick a "gonnegtion," dwells on the memory of the shooting of Rosy Rosenthal, runs the Swastika Holding Company, and refuses to attend Gatsby's funeral. Walter Chase went to jail rather than inform on Gatsby because he feared Wolfsheim.

**Gatsby's parties**
The lavish parties at Gatsby's West Egg mansion, which a "small eyesore" neighbor, Nick, describes as an imitation "Hotel de Ville in Normandy." Five crates of oranges and lemons arrive every Friday, the orchestra plays Vladimir Tostoff's "Jazz History of the World," and after one party two men crash into a ditch when their car loses a wheel. Nick first meets Gatsby at one of these parties.

**Owl Eyes and "a regular Belasco"**
A drunk partygoer with owl-eyed spectacles who is amazed that the books in Gatsby's "Merton College Library" are real, not cardboard, and calls Gatsby "a regular Belasco," after the theatrical producer David Belasco, known for realistic stage sets. He is one of the few people who come to Gatsby's funeral.

**"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past"**
The novel's famous last line. In the final scene Nick lies on the beach and imagines the "transitory enchanted moment" when Dutch sailors first saw the "fresh, green breast of the new world." The novel opens with Nick recalling his father's advice to remember that not everyone has had his advantages, and its epigraph is attributed to the fictional poet Thomas Parke D'Invilliers.

**James Gatz and Dan Cody**
Gatsby was born James Gatz to poor farmers in North Dakota and briefly attended St. Olaf College in Minnesota. As a teenager he rowed out on Lake Superior to warn the millionaire Dan Cody that his yacht was in danger, and Cody hired him. Gatsby was supposed to inherit Cody's money, but it went to Cody's mistress Ella Kaye. Nick says Gatsby "sprang from his Platonic conception of himself."

**"Old sport," Oxford, and the Montenegro medal**
Gatsby constantly calls people "old sport." To back up his claims of a noble past, he shows Nick a medal from Montenegro inscribed "Nicolas Rex" and a photograph from Oxford. He later admits he attended Oxford for only five months after the war, so he "can't really call [himself] an Oxford man." Rumors at his parties include that he killed a man and that he is related to Kaiser Wilhelm.

**Jordan Baker**
Daisy's friend, a professional golfer who once cheated in a tournament and is habitually dishonest, which Nick finds attractive. She first appears with Daisy lying on a couch in white dresses, holding herself as if balancing something on her chin. When Nick criticizes her careless driving she replies that "it takes two to make an accident." Nghi Vo's novel The Chosen and the Beautiful retells the story from her point of view.

**The shirts scene**
When Gatsby shows Daisy his mansion, he throws piles of his expensive shirts onto the table, and Daisy sobs into them, saying she has never seen such beautiful shirts. Gatsby's resident freeloader Klipspringer plays the piano that day, and later calls Nick about his tennis shoes instead of attending the funeral.

**The Plaza Hotel confrontation**
On a hot afternoon in Manhattan, Tom confronts Gatsby over Daisy and exposes his bootlegging, and Daisy cannot say she never loved Tom. Nick realizes that it is his thirtieth birthday. Tom then sends Daisy home with Gatsby in Gatsby's car, which leads directly to Myrtle's death. Earlier, Daisy had told Gatsby "you always look so cool," revealing her love in front of Tom.

**The party at Myrtle's Manhattan apartment**
Nick gets drunk for the second time in his life at the apartment Tom keeps for Myrtle, along with the McKees and Myrtle's sister Catherine. Catherine repeats the rumor that Gatsby is related to Kaiser Wilhelm and falsely claims that Daisy is Catholic to explain why Tom won't get a divorce. A photo there looks like a hen on a blurred rock. Tom, who hates the word "hulking," breaks Myrtle's nose here when she says Daisy's name.

**Henry C. Gatz and the Hopalong Cassidy schedule**
At Gatsby's poorly attended funeral, his father Henry C. Gatz shows Nick an old copy of Hopalong Cassidy in which the young James Gatz wrote a daily schedule and a list of "General Resolves" for improving himself.
